questiontext.text: A test plan is best described as:

answer.text: A document describing the scope, objectives, approach, resources and schedule of the intended test activities

feedback.text: Correct — the test plan is the output of test planning and sets out what will be tested, how, by whom, and when.

answer.text: A list of the concrete inputs and expected results for one specific test

feedback.text: That describes a single test case, not the overall test plan.

answer.text: A record of a single failure observed while running the software

feedback.text: That is a defect (incident) report, produced during execution.

answer.text: The source code of the program under test

feedback.text: The code is part of the test object, not the test plan.

generalfeedback.text: Test planning is the first activity of the fundamental test process; its work product, the test plan, defines the objectives, scope, approach, resources and schedule for testing.

questiontext.text: The test basis is:

answer.text: The body of knowledge (requirements, specifications, designs, user stories, risk reports) used as the basis for analysing and designing tests

feedback.text: Correct — tests are derived from the test basis.

answer.text: The minimum set of tests that must pass before release

feedback.text: That is closer to an exit criterion or a smoke-test set, not the test basis.

answer.text: The hardware and software environment in which tests are executed

feedback.text: That is the test environment, not the test basis.

answer.text: The team of people responsible for testing

feedback.text: People are resources; the test basis is the source material tests are derived from.

generalfeedback.text: The test basis is everything a test is derived from — requirements, specifications, design and implementation information, user stories, risk analyses and so on. Test analysis works from it to determine what to test.

questiontext.text: A test condition is:

answer.text: A testable aspect of the test basis (a feature, function, requirement or quality attribute) that a test could exercise

feedback.text: Correct — test conditions say WHAT should be tested; they are identified during test analysis.

answer.text: The concrete input values and expected outputs of a runnable test

feedback.text: Those belong to a test case, which is designed later from a test condition.

answer.text: The state the system must be in before a test can start

feedback.text: That is a precondition of a test case, not a test condition.

answer.text: A defect found during execution

feedback.text: A defect is an observed failure/fault, not a test condition.

generalfeedback.text: A test condition is an item or aspect of the test basis (a function, requirement, or quality characteristic) worth testing. It answers “what to test” and is the output of test analysis; the concrete test case is designed from it afterwards.

questiontext.text: A test case is:

answer.text: A set of preconditions, inputs, expected results and postconditions developed to exercise a test condition

feedback.text: Correct — a test case makes a test condition concrete and executable.

answer.text: A high-level statement of an aspect of the test basis worth testing

feedback.text: That is a test condition; a test case is derived from it and is concrete.

answer.text: The overall schedule and resourcing document for testing

feedback.text: That is the test plan.

answer.text: The end-of-project summary of how testing went

feedback.text: That is the test summary report, produced at test completion.

generalfeedback.text: A test case turns a test condition into something you can run: it specifies preconditions, inputs, the expected results to compare against, and postconditions. It is the main work product of test design.

name.text: What a test case must contain

questiontext.text: Which element is essential to a well-formed test case?

answer.text: The expected result to compare the actual result against

feedback.text: Correct — without a documented expected result you cannot decide pass or fail (the oracle problem).

answer.text: The name of the developer who wrote the code

feedback.text: Useful metadata perhaps, but not an essential part of a test case.

answer.text: A guarantee that the test will pass

feedback.text: A test case is not required to pass; it must have a defined expected result.

answer.text: The total project budget

feedback.text: Budget is a planning concern, not part of a test case.

generalfeedback.text: A test case specifies preconditions, inputs, expected results and postconditions. The expected result is essential: comparing the actual result to a predefined expected result is what makes a verdict (pass/fail) possible.

questiontext.text: Entry criteria for a test activity are:

answer.text: The conditions that must be satisfied before that activity can sensibly begin

feedback.text: Correct — entry criteria gate the START of an activity (a “definition of ready”).

answer.text: The conditions that must be met before testing can be declared finished

feedback.text: Those are exit criteria, which gate the stop, not the start.

answer.text: The list of defects still open at the end of testing

feedback.text: That is residual-defect data, not entry criteria.

answer.text: The inputs of a single test case

feedback.text: Those are test-case inputs, not entry criteria for an activity.

generalfeedback.text: Entry criteria define what must be in place before an activity starts — e.g. a stable build deployed, the test environment ready, and test data available. They are checked at the start of test implementation/execution.

questiontext.text: Exit criteria for testing are:

answer.text: The conditions that must be met before testing can be considered complete for the agreed objectives

feedback.text: Correct — exit criteria gate the STOP (a “definition of done” for testing).

answer.text: The conditions that must be met before testing can begin

feedback.text: Those are entry criteria, which gate the start.

answer.text: The list of stakeholders who approved the test plan

feedback.text: Approval sign-off is not the same as exit criteria.

answer.text: The set of test conditions produced by test analysis

feedback.text: Those are analysis outputs, not exit criteria.

generalfeedback.text: Exit criteria (completion criteria) state when testing is done — e.g. planned coverage achieved, no unresolved high-severity defects, and the time/budget consumed. They are checked during test monitoring & control and at completion.

questiontext.text: A test procedure (test script) is:

answer.text: A sequence of actions and test cases arranged in the order they will be executed, with any needed setup

feedback.text: Correct — the test procedure specifies the execution steps and ordering; it is built during test implementation.

answer.text: A high-level aspect of the test basis worth testing

feedback.text: That is a test condition.

answer.text: The overall objectives and schedule for the whole test effort

feedback.text: That is the test plan.

answer.text: A report on how many tests passed

feedback.text: That is a test result / summary, not a procedure.

generalfeedback.text: A test procedure specifies the sequence of steps (and the test cases in execution order) to run tests, including preconditions and setup. Producing test procedures is part of test implementation.

questiontext.text: A test suite is:

answer.text: A collection of test cases or test procedures grouped together to be run as a set

feedback.text: Correct — a suite bundles related tests for execution and reporting.

answer.text: A single input/expected-result pair

feedback.text: That is one test case, not a suite of them.

answer.text: The requirements document the tests are derived from

feedback.text: That is part of the test basis.

answer.text: A tool that measures code coverage

feedback.text: That is a coverage tool, not a test suite.

generalfeedback.text: A test suite groups test cases/procedures for execution (for example a smoke suite or a regression suite). Organising tests into suites happens during test implementation.

questiontext.text: A defect (incident) report primarily records:

answer.text: An observed anomaly (the discrepancy between actual and expected behaviour) so it can be investigated and tracked

feedback.text: Correct — defect reports are logged during execution and drive the defect lifecycle.

answer.text: The planned scope and schedule of testing

feedback.text: That is the test plan.

answer.text: The list of test conditions to be covered

feedback.text: Those come from test analysis, not from a defect report.

answer.text: A guarantee that the software is defect-free

feedback.text: Testing cannot prove the absence of defects; a defect report records a specific anomaly found.

generalfeedback.text: When actual behaviour differs from expected behaviour during execution, the tester logs a defect report describing the anomaly, how to reproduce it, and its impact. This starts the defect lifecycle.

name.text: Correct order of the main activities

questiontext.text: Ignoring the continuous monitoring & control activity, which sequence gives the correct order of the fundamental test process activities?

answer.text: Planning, analysis, design, implementation, execution, completion

feedback.text: Correct — this is the canonical order (with monitoring & control running throughout).

answer.text: Planning, design, analysis, execution, implementation, completion

feedback.text: Analysis (what to test) must precede design (how to test), and implementation must precede execution.

answer.text: Analysis, planning, design, execution, implementation, completion

feedback.text: Planning comes first, and implementation precedes execution.

answer.text: Planning, analysis, design, execution, implementation, completion

feedback.text: Implementation (building procedures/data/environment) precedes execution, not the other way round.

generalfeedback.text: The fundamental test process runs: test planning → test analysis → test design → test implementation → test execution → test completion, with test monitoring & control as a continuous activity spanning all of them.

questiontext.text: Actually running the tests, comparing actual results to expected results, and logging defects is done in:

answer.text: Test execution

feedback.text: Correct — execution runs the tests and records the outcomes and any defects.

answer.text: Test analysis

feedback.text: Analysis identifies test conditions; it does not run tests.

answer.text: Test design

feedback.text: Design produces test cases; it does not run them.

answer.text: Test planning

feedback.text: Planning sets scope and approach; running tests happens much later.

generalfeedback.text: Test execution is the activity where test suites are run, actual results are compared with expected results, discrepancies are logged as defects, and confirmation/regression testing takes place.

questiontext.text: The main purpose of test completion (test closure) is to:

answer.text: Wrap up testing — report results, finalise and archive testware, and capture lessons learned

feedback.text: Correct — completion consolidates and hands over the outcomes of testing.

answer.text: Identify the test conditions from the test basis

feedback.text: That is test analysis, near the start of the process.

answer.text: Write the concrete inputs and expected results of each test

feedback.text: That is test design.

answer.text: Run the test suites for the first time

feedback.text: That is test execution, which precedes completion.

generalfeedback.text: Test completion happens when a milestone is reached (release, end of iteration, project close). It gathers data, produces a test summary report, finalises and archives testware, hands it over, and records lessons learned.

questiontext.text: Test monitoring and control is:

answer.text: An ongoing activity that compares actual progress against the plan and takes corrective action throughout testing

feedback.text: Correct — it runs continuously, not just once, and steers the effort.

answer.text: A one-off activity done only at the very end of the project

feedback.text: That would be closer to completion; monitoring & control is continuous.

answer.text: The activity that derives test cases from test conditions

feedback.text: That is test design.

answer.text: The activity that logs each individual defect

feedback.text: Defects are logged during execution; monitoring uses that data to steer.

generalfeedback.text: Test monitoring & control runs throughout the whole process: monitoring gathers information (progress, coverage, defect data) and control uses it to guide testing so exit criteria can be met.

questiontext.text: Test analysis determines what to test by identifying test conditions from the test basis.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — analysis works from the test basis to identify and prioritise test conditions (the “what”); designing the “how” comes next.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: It is true: test analysis identifies test conditions (what to test); test design then produces the test cases (how to test).

generalfeedback.text: Test analysis analyses the test basis to determine what to test, producing test conditions. Test design then turns those conditions into concrete test cases.

questiontext.text: In the fundamental test process, which activity immediately precedes test design?

answer.text: Test analysis

feedback.text: Correct — analysis identifies the test conditions that design then turns into test cases.

answer.text: Test implementation

feedback.text: Implementation follows design, not precedes it.

answer.text: Test execution

feedback.text: Execution comes much later, after implementation.

answer.text: Test completion

feedback.text: Completion is the last activity, not before design.

generalfeedback.text: The order is analysis → design → implementation. Test design consumes the test conditions produced by test analysis.

questiontext.text: Which activity immediately follows test design?

answer.text: Test implementation

feedback.text: Correct — after the test cases are designed, implementation builds the procedures, suites, data and environment.

answer.text: Test analysis

feedback.text: Analysis precedes design, not follows it.

answer.text: Test execution

feedback.text: Execution comes after implementation, not directly after design.

answer.text: Test planning

feedback.text: Planning is the first activity, not after design.

generalfeedback.text: Analysis → design → implementation → execution. Implementation directly follows design: it makes the designed tests runnable.

questiontext.text: Which activity immediately follows test implementation?

answer.text: Test execution

feedback.text: Correct — once the testware and environment are ready and entry criteria are met, the tests are executed.

answer.text: Test design

feedback.text: Design precedes implementation.

answer.text: Test analysis

feedback.text: Analysis is earlier still.

answer.text: Test completion

feedback.text: Completion comes after execution, not directly after implementation.

generalfeedback.text: Implementation → execution: implementation finalises the testware, data and environment (and checks readiness/entry criteria); execution then runs the tests.

name.text: Naming the activity from its work

questiontext.text: “Analyse the test basis to determine testable features and derive test conditions.” This describes:

answer.text: Test analysis

feedback.text: Correct — evaluating the test basis and producing test conditions is exactly test analysis.

answer.text: Test design

feedback.text: Design turns those conditions into test cases; it does not derive the conditions.

answer.text: Test planning

feedback.text: Planning sets scope and approach; it does not analyse the basis into conditions.

answer.text: Test implementation

feedback.text: Implementation builds procedures and data; it does not derive test conditions.

generalfeedback.text: Test analysis evaluates the test basis, identifies testable features, and defines and prioritises test conditions — the “what to test”.

questiontext.text: Which of the following is an entry criterion for starting test execution?

answer.text: A stable, testable build is deployed and the test environment and test data are ready

feedback.text: Correct — that must hold before execution can meaningfully begin.

answer.text: Planned requirements coverage has been achieved

feedback.text: That is an exit criterion — it describes when to stop, not when to start.

answer.text: No high-severity defects remain open

feedback.text: That is an exit criterion, evaluated to decide completion.

answer.text: The test summary report has been signed off

feedback.text: That happens at completion, well after execution starts.

generalfeedback.text: Entry criteria gate the start: a deployable build, a ready environment and available test data are typical entry criteria for execution. Coverage achieved and no open high-severity defects are exit criteria.

questiontext.text: Which of the following is an exit criterion for testing?

answer.text: All planned test cases have been executed and the required coverage target has been met

feedback.text: Correct — that is a completion condition, checked to decide whether to stop.

answer.text: The test environment has been provisioned

feedback.text: That is an entry criterion for execution.

answer.text: The requirements specification is available

feedback.text: That enables analysis/design to start; it is an entry-side precondition, not an exit criterion.

answer.text: Test data has been prepared

feedback.text: That is an entry-side readiness condition, not an exit criterion.

generalfeedback.text: Exit (completion) criteria describe when testing is done: e.g. planned tests executed, coverage targets met, defect levels acceptable, and time/budget consumed.

questiontext.text: Fill the blank in the derivation chain: test basis → ______ → test cases.

answer.text: Test conditions

feedback.text: Correct — analysis derives test conditions from the basis, then design derives test cases from the conditions.

answer.text: Defect reports

feedback.text: Defect reports come from execution, not between the basis and the test cases.

answer.text: Test suites

feedback.text: Test suites group cases during implementation; they are not the step between basis and cases.

answer.text: Exit criteria

feedback.text: Exit criteria are completion conditions, not a derivation step.

generalfeedback.text: The flow is test basis → test conditions (analysis) → test cases (design) → test procedures/suites (implementation) → execution → defects → closure.

questiontext.text: After a developer fixes a reported defect, confirmation (re-)testing means:

answer.text: Re-executing the test that originally failed to confirm the defect is now fixed

feedback.text: Correct — confirmation testing verifies the specific fix.

answer.text: Running a broad set of other tests to check nothing else broke

feedback.text: That is regression testing, a different purpose.

answer.text: Writing a new test condition from the requirements

feedback.text: That is test analysis, unrelated to confirming a fix.

answer.text: Reviewing the requirements document for defects

feedback.text: That is static verification of a work product, not confirmation testing of a fix.

generalfeedback.text: Confirmation testing (re-testing) re-runs the previously failing test after the fix, to confirm the original defect has been removed. Regression testing separately checks that the change did not break anything else.

questiontext.text: The purpose of regression testing is to:

answer.text: Detect whether a change has broken previously working functionality

feedback.text: Correct — regression testing guards against unintended side effects of changes.

answer.text: Confirm that a specific reported defect has been fixed

feedback.text: That is confirmation (re-)testing, not regression testing.

answer.text: Determine which test conditions to cover

feedback.text: That is test analysis.

answer.text: Provision the test environment

feedback.text: That is part of test implementation.

generalfeedback.text: A change (a fix or new feature) can have side effects. Regression testing re-runs existing tests on unchanged areas to detect such unintended breakages, whereas confirmation testing verifies the intended fix itself.

questiontext.text: Maintaining traceability from test basis items to test conditions, test cases and results mainly enables you to:

answer.text: Measure coverage of the test basis and assess the impact of changes

feedback.text: Correct — traceability shows which requirements are covered and what to re-test when something changes.

answer.text: Guarantee that the software contains no defects

feedback.text: No amount of tracing can prove the absence of defects.

answer.text: Remove the need for exit criteria

feedback.text: Traceability supports evaluating exit criteria; it does not replace them.

answer.text: Speed up the compiler

feedback.text: Traceability is about relating work products, not build performance.

generalfeedback.text: Bidirectional traceability links requirements/test basis ↔ test conditions ↔ test cases ↔ results/defects. It supports coverage measurement, impact analysis for changes, and meaningful progress reporting.

questiontext.text: In a typical defect lifecycle, immediately after the defect is marked fixed/resolved by the developer, the tester should:

answer.text: Re-test (confirmation test) the fix and, if it passes, move the defect toward closed

feedback.text: Correct — the fix must be confirmed before the defect can be closed.

answer.text: Immediately close the defect without re-running any test

feedback.text: A fix should be confirmed by re-testing before closing.

answer.text: Delete the defect report

feedback.text: Reports are retained for history and metrics, not deleted.

answer.text: Reassign it to the requirements author

feedback.text: A resolved defect goes to the tester for confirmation, not back to requirements.

generalfeedback.text: A common lifecycle is new → assigned → fixed → retest (confirmation) → closed, with a reopen path if the retest fails. The tester confirms the fix before closure.

questiontext.text: When a tester first logs an anomaly during execution, the defect typically enters which state?

answer.text: New (open), awaiting triage/assignment

feedback.text: Correct — a freshly reported defect starts as new/open before being assigned.

answer.text: Closed

feedback.text: Closed is the end state, reached after a confirmed fix.

answer.text: Fixed

feedback.text: Fixed comes after a developer resolves it, not at first report.

answer.text: Retest passed

feedback.text: That occurs only after a fix has been confirmed.

generalfeedback.text: The lifecycle usually begins new/open → assigned → in progress → fixed → retest → closed (with reopen/reject/defer branches). A newly logged defect is new/open.

name.text: Activity that produces procedures and checks readiness

questiontext.text: Building test procedures and suites, preparing test data and the environment, and checking that entry criteria/readiness are met belongs to:

answer.text: Test implementation

feedback.text: Correct — implementation makes the designed tests runnable and confirms everything is ready to execute.

answer.text: Test design

feedback.text: Design produces the test cases; organising procedures/data/environment is implementation.

answer.text: Test execution

feedback.text: Execution runs the tests; the preparation of testware and environment precedes it.

answer.text: Test completion

feedback.text: Completion wraps up testing after execution.

generalfeedback.text: Test implementation organises testware for execution: it creates/finalises test procedures and suites, prepares test data and the environment, and verifies readiness (entry criteria) before execution starts.

name.text: Activity that builds test cases from conditions

questiontext.text: Turning test conditions into concrete test cases (with inputs and expected results) is the job of:

answer.text: Test design

feedback.text: Correct — design elaborates test conditions into runnable test cases; the “how to test”.

answer.text: Test analysis

feedback.text: Analysis produces the test conditions; design turns them into test cases.

answer.text: Test implementation

feedback.text: Implementation sequences and organises the cases; it does not first create them from conditions.

answer.text: Test monitoring and control

feedback.text: That steers the effort; it does not design test cases.

generalfeedback.text: Test design takes the test conditions from analysis and designs test cases and sets of test cases (inputs, expected results, coverage items) — the “how to test”.

questiontext.text: Confirmation testing is normally performed before the defect has been fixed.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — confirmation testing re-runs the failing test AFTER the fix, to confirm the defect is gone.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: It is false: there is nothing to confirm until the fix has been made; confirmation testing follows the fix.

generalfeedback.text: Confirmation (re-)testing is done after a fix is delivered, re-executing the previously failing test to confirm the defect has been resolved.

questiontext.text: A colleague lists the sequential activities scrambled as: execution, planning, design, completion, implementation, analysis. Put them back into the correct order.

answer.text: Planning, analysis, design, implementation, execution, completion

feedback.text: Correct — the canonical sequential order of the fundamental test process.

answer.text: Planning, analysis, design, execution, implementation, completion

feedback.text: Implementation must precede execution — you cannot run tests before the testware and environment are ready.

answer.text: Planning, design, analysis, implementation, execution, completion

feedback.text: Analysis (what to test) must come before design (how to test).

answer.text: Analysis, planning, design, implementation, execution, completion

feedback.text: Planning is the first activity, before analysis.

generalfeedback.text: Sequentially: planning → analysis → design → implementation → execution → completion (with monitoring & control throughout). Watch the two common traps: analysis before design, and implementation before execution.

questiontext.text: Why are agreed exit criteria important to the test process?

answer.text: They give an objective, agreed basis for deciding when to stop testing, rather than stopping arbitrarily

feedback.text: Correct — testing is potentially endless, so exit criteria define “done” up front.

answer.text: They guarantee that the product is completely defect-free once met

feedback.text: Meeting exit criteria never proves the absence of defects.

answer.text: They remove the need to plan or monitor testing

feedback.text: Exit criteria are set during planning and evaluated during monitoring & control; they do not replace them.

answer.text: They decide which test conditions to derive from the basis

feedback.text: That is test analysis, unrelated to stopping.

generalfeedback.text: Because exhaustive testing is impossible, exit (completion) criteria provide an agreed, measurable basis for deciding when enough testing has been done, supporting a rational stop/continue decision.

questiontext.text: Which of the following is least appropriate as an exit criterion for testing?

answer.text: The test environment has been installed and the build deployed

feedback.text: Correct — that is an entry/readiness condition; it says nothing about whether testing is complete.

answer.text: The planned coverage target has been achieved

feedback.text: That is a legitimate exit criterion.

answer.text: The residual defect rate is within the agreed threshold

feedback.text: That is a legitimate exit criterion.

answer.text: The allotted test time/budget has been consumed

feedback.text: Time/budget is a commonly used (if blunt) exit criterion.

generalfeedback.text: Exit criteria describe completion — coverage achieved, defect levels acceptable, time/budget consumed. “Environment installed / build deployed” is an entry-side readiness condition, not a measure of whether testing is finished.

name.text: Who produces the test summary report

questiontext.text: The test summary report is produced as part of which activity?

answer.text: Test completion

feedback.text: Correct — the summary report is a completion work product that consolidates the results.

answer.text: Test planning

feedback.text: Planning produces the test plan, not the summary report.

answer.text: Test analysis

feedback.text: Analysis produces test conditions.

answer.text: Test execution

feedback.text: Execution produces logs and defect reports; the consolidated summary is written at completion.

generalfeedback.text: Test completion gathers data from finished activities and produces the test summary report for stakeholders, alongside archiving testware and capturing lessons learned.

questiontext.text: Which work product is the primary output of test analysis?

answer.text: (Prioritised) test conditions

feedback.text: Correct — analysis evaluates the basis and yields test conditions.

answer.text: Test cases with concrete inputs and expected results

feedback.text: Those are the output of test design.

answer.text: Test procedures and suites ready to run

feedback.text: Those come from test implementation.

answer.text: The test summary report

feedback.text: That comes from test completion.

generalfeedback.text: Each activity has characteristic work products: analysis → test conditions; design → test cases; implementation → test procedures/suites, data, environment; execution → results/defect reports; completion → summary report and archived testware.

questiontext.text: Which statement best distinguishes test monitoring & control from test planning?

answer.text: Planning sets out the intended approach up front; monitoring & control continuously compares actual progress with the plan and takes corrective action

feedback.text: Correct — planning defines the plan; monitoring & control keeps testing on track against it.

answer.text: They are the same activity under two different names

feedback.text: They are distinct: one defines the plan, the other continuously steers against it.

answer.text: Planning happens continuously while monitoring & control happens only at the start

feedback.text: It is the reverse: monitoring & control is the continuous one.

answer.text: Monitoring & control derives the test cases from test conditions

feedback.text: That is test design, not monitoring & control.

generalfeedback.text: Planning is largely done up front (and revised as needed) and yields the plan. Monitoring & control is a continuous activity: it measures progress/coverage/defects against the plan and applies control actions (e.g. re-prioritising, reallocating) to meet the exit criteria.

questiontext.text: Which of the following is a genuine test completion activity?

answer.text: Analysing lessons learned and archiving the testware for future reuse

feedback.text: Correct — capturing lessons learned and archiving/handing over testware are classic completion tasks.

answer.text: Deriving test conditions from the requirements

feedback.text: That is test analysis, near the start of the process.

answer.text: Preparing test data and provisioning the environment

feedback.text: That is test implementation.

answer.text: Comparing actual results with expected results

feedback.text: That is test execution.

generalfeedback.text: Test completion activities include: checking all defects are closed/deferred, creating the test summary report, finalising and archiving testware, handing it over, and capturing lessons learned for process improvement.

name.text: Subtle: which activity organises the suite

questiontext.text: “Group the finished test cases into an executable regression suite, sequence them, and load the required test data.” This is:

answer.text: Test implementation

feedback.text: Correct — organising cases into runnable suites/procedures with data prepared is implementation.

answer.text: Test design

feedback.text: Design creates the cases; grouping/sequencing them for execution is implementation.

answer.text: Test analysis

feedback.text: Analysis identifies conditions, not runnable suites.

answer.text: Test execution

feedback.text: Execution runs the suite; assembling and loading it is the preceding implementation step.

generalfeedback.text: Once test cases exist (design), implementation sequences them into test procedures/suites, prepares data and environment, and confirms readiness. Only then does execution run them.

questiontext.text: “Review the requirements and risk report, list the testable features, and rank the resulting test conditions by risk.” This is:

answer.text: Test analysis

feedback.text: Correct — identifying and prioritising test conditions from the basis is analysis.

answer.text: Test design

feedback.text: Design comes next, converting the prioritised conditions into test cases.

answer.text: Test planning

feedback.text: Planning sets overall strategy; deriving and ranking conditions is analysis.

answer.text: Test monitoring and control

feedback.text: That steers progress; it does not derive test conditions.

generalfeedback.text: Test analysis evaluates the test basis (including risk information), identifies testable features, and defines and prioritises test conditions — still the “what”, not yet the “how”.

name.text: Subtle: specifying inputs and expected results

questiontext.text: “For the test condition ‘withdrawal exceeds balance’, specify the account state, the amount to withdraw, and the exact expected error message.” This is:

answer.text: Test design

feedback.text: Correct — turning a condition into concrete inputs, preconditions and expected results is design.

answer.text: Test analysis

feedback.text: Analysis produced the condition; specifying concrete inputs/expected results is design.

answer.text: Test implementation

feedback.text: Implementation would then sequence and prepare this case for execution; it does not first specify its inputs/expected results.

answer.text: Test execution

feedback.text: Execution runs the case; here we are still designing it.

generalfeedback.text: Deriving concrete preconditions, inputs and expected results from a test condition is exactly test design (the “how”). Analysis gave the condition; implementation later makes the case runnable.

name.text: Verification of work products vs execution

questiontext.text: Reviewing a requirements specification for ambiguities and contradictions, before any code is run, is best characterised as:

answer.text: Static verification of a work product, which can begin during test analysis

feedback.text: Correct — reviewing the test basis is static work and often surfaces defects early, before dynamic execution.

answer.text: Test execution, because a defect was found

feedback.text: Execution requires running the software; reviewing a document is static, not dynamic.

answer.text: Confirmation testing of a fix

feedback.text: There is no fix being re-tested here; this is a static review.

answer.text: Test completion, because it wraps things up

feedback.text: Reviewing the basis happens early, not at closure.

generalfeedback.text: Verification checks whether a work product meets its specification and can be done statically (reviews, static analysis) without executing code. Reviewing the test basis often happens as part of/around test analysis and can find defects before dynamic execution begins.

name.text: When exit criteria are not met

questiontext.text: Monitoring shows that, at the planned end date, the agreed exit criteria are not yet met. Which response is most consistent with the test process?

answer.text: Report the status and, via control, decide to continue testing or renegotiate the criteria/scope with stakeholders

feedback.text: Correct — unmet exit criteria feed a control decision; you do not simply declare done.

answer.text: Automatically declare testing complete because the date arrived

feedback.text: A calendar date alone does not satisfy exit criteria; that ignores the criteria's purpose.

answer.text: Delete the failing tests so the criteria appear satisfied

feedback.text: Gaming the metric hides risk; it is not a legitimate response.

answer.text: Skip straight to archiving testware without any report

feedback.text: Completion still requires reporting; and the decision to stop must be made explicitly.

generalfeedback.text: Exit criteria drive a stop/continue decision. If they are unmet, monitoring & control reports the situation and stakeholders decide to continue testing, add resources, or consciously accept the risk by renegotiating scope/criteria — never by pretending they are met.

questiontext.text: Within the continuous activity, which is a control action rather than a monitoring action?

answer.text: Re-prioritising the remaining tests and reassigning testers because a risky area is behind

feedback.text: Correct — taking corrective action to steer the effort is control.

answer.text: Measuring how many planned test cases have run so far

feedback.text: That is monitoring — gathering information, not acting on it.

answer.text: Recording the current defect find/fix counts

feedback.text: That is monitoring (collecting data).

answer.text: Reporting coverage progress against the plan

feedback.text: That is monitoring/reporting, not a corrective action.

generalfeedback.text: Monitoring gathers and reports information (progress, coverage, defect data); control uses that information to take corrective actions — re-prioritising, reallocating resources, adjusting the schedule — so that the exit criteria can still be met.

questiontext.text: Which pairing of an activity with its characteristic work product is incorrect?

answer.text: Test execution produces the test conditions

feedback.text: Correct — this pairing is wrong: test conditions come from test analysis, not execution.

answer.text: Test design produces test cases

feedback.text: This pairing is correct, so it is not the answer.

answer.text: Test implementation produces test procedures and suites

feedback.text: This pairing is correct, so it is not the answer.

answer.text: Test completion produces the test summary report

feedback.text: This pairing is correct, so it is not the answer.

generalfeedback.text: Characteristic work products: analysis → test conditions; design → test cases; implementation → test procedures/suites, data, environment; execution → test logs and defect reports; completion → test summary report. Execution does not produce test conditions.

name.text: Entry gates start, exit gates stop

questiontext.text: Entry criteria gate the start of a test activity, whereas exit criteria gate its completion.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — entry criteria are the “definition of ready” to begin; exit criteria are the “definition of done” to stop.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: It is true: entry criteria must hold before an activity begins; exit criteria must hold before it is declared complete.

generalfeedback.text: Entry criteria (readiness) must be satisfied before an activity such as execution starts; exit/completion criteria must be satisfied before testing is considered finished. Confusing the two is a common error.
